subtitle: Secondary traumatic stress, vicarious trauma, compassion fatigue and burnout are related but different. Learn to tell them apart and take organizational, supervisory and personal steps that sustain people doing hard work.
audience: For all DHS and DSD employees whose work involves difficult material, including case managers, intake, incident review, licensing, policy and communications staff, and for supervisors who shape how that work is organized.

lessons.title: Naming the strain: secondary traumatic stress, vicarious trauma, compassion fatigue and burnout
objectives: Distinguish secondary traumatic stress, vicarious trauma, compassion fatigue and burnout in plain language.
Identify ways DHS and DSD work exposes staff to other people's trauma, including indirect exposure.
Explain why these terms describe work experiences rather than diagnoses of colleagues.
Describe compassion satisfaction and vicarious resilience as part of the same picture.
lessons.teaching:
People who work in human services carry other people's hardest moments. At DHS and DSD that can mean reading maltreatment reports, taking calls from families in crisis, reviewing a death or serious injury, investigating a provider, reading public comments full of grief or anger, or hearing, again and again, what a system failure meant for someone's life. You do not have to be in the room when something terrible happens for it to affect you. People respond differently, and prior experiences may affect how work feels. Do not infer someone’s response from their identity or family background.

Several terms describe what can happen, and they overlap. The National Child Traumatic Stress Network describes secondary traumatic stress as distress associated with hearing about another person’s trauma, an occupational concern in child-serving work. Vicarious trauma, as the federal Office for Victims of Crime describes it, is an occupational challenge that comes from continuous exposure to other people's trauma; over time it can produce a range of negative psychological and social reactions. Compassion fatigue is often used as an umbrella term; SAMHSA describes it as a combination of burnout and secondary traumatic stress. Burnout, in the World Health Organization's definition, is a syndrome resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed, marked by exhaustion, mental distance or cynicism about the job, and reduced sense of effectiveness. WHO classifies burnout as an occupational phenomenon, not a medical condition. Burnout can come from workload and conditions without any trauma exposure.

The same work also brings meaning. Compassion satisfaction is the sense of fulfillment that comes from helping, and vicarious resilience describes the strength some workers draw from witnessing how people recover and adapt. Both can exist alongside strain.

These concepts help explain possible effects of work; they do not let coworkers determine a person’s condition or its cause. A clinician can assess health concerns. Ordinary team discussion should not pressure people to disclose health information or trauma history. Formal accommodation, leave or safety processes may require limited information through authorized channels. What matters for a team is noticing the conditions of the work, such as exposure, workload and support, and changing what can be changed. The rest of this course treats sustaining the work as a shared responsibility, not a test of personal toughness.
lessons.keyPoint: These concepts describe different forms of work-related strain. Discuss working conditions without assigning a health label to a colleague, and respond to concrete work or safety concerns.
lessons.example: Practice case: Jada works in a DSD unit that reviews reports of serious incidents involving people receiving waiver services. After a hard month, she tells a coworker, Ben, that she has stopped reading the full reports and just skims for the required fields. Ben replies that she sounds burned out and should probably see someone. Jada says she is fine and just busy. Later, Ben wonders whether he should tell their supervisor that Jada has secondary trauma. Required report completeness is being checked through the supervisor’s normal quality process. Ben is considering how to offer support alongside that work, not whether to ignore a missed duty.
lessons.question: What should Ben do next?
choices: Tell the supervisor that Jada has secondary trauma so she can be taken off incident reviews.
Drop it completely, since Jada said she was fine.
Check in with Jada without labeling her, mention that the work has been heavy for everyone, and suggest raising workload and exposure at the next team meeting.
feedback: Ben should report concrete work concerns through the appropriate route, without claiming a diagnosis or deciding that Jada should lose an assignment. Share necessary facts rather than a speculative health label.
Respecting her answer matters, but the heavy month is a team condition worth raising. Ben can do that without singling Jada out.

This is the strongest supportive response alongside the quality review already underway. Ben can check in without pressure to disclose, and discuss team workload without naming Jada. Urgent safety, reporting or service obligations must not wait for a team meeting.
lessons.reflection: Which parts of your work bring you closest to other people's suffering, even indirectly? Which parts bring you a sense of meaning?
lessons.action: List the main ways your role exposes you to difficult material, such as reports, calls, files, reviews or public comments. Note which ones arrive without warning, and bring one idea for predictability or support to your next check-in with your supervisor.

check.question: How does the World Health Organization classify burnout?
check.correct: As an occupational phenomenon resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed, not as a medical condition.
wrong: As a mental illness that requires a clinical diagnosis.
As the same thing as secondary traumatic stress.
check.feedback: WHO describes burnout as specific to the work context, with exhaustion, mental distance or cynicism, and reduced effectiveness. It can occur without trauma exposure, which is why it is distinct from secondary traumatic stress.

lessons.title: Why the response must be organizational
objectives: Explain the demands and resources view of burnout used by NIOSH.
Identify organizational conditions that increase or reduce strain in DHS and DSD work.
Compare individual coping advice with changes that teams and leaders can make.
Plan one change to how difficult material reaches a team.
lessons.teaching:
Personal recovery practices may help, but they cannot by themselves correct excessive demands or inadequate resources at work. The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, in its burnout training for public health supervisors and managers, frames burnout as a mismatch between demands and resources: too many demands that require effort, and not enough of what people need to meet them. Resources include time, staffing, clear information, decision authority, trust and support. When the mismatch is chronic, it creates what NIOSH calls drain cycles. The Office for Victims of Crime's toolkit likewise stresses that organizations have roles and responsibilities in addressing vicarious trauma, not only individual workers.

This matters for fairness as well as health. If well-being is treated only as a personal matter, the people who struggle are blamed for conditions they did not create. Caregiving, access barriers and experiences outside work may affect what support a person needs. Ask about workable conditions rather than assuming a burden or resilience level from someone’s circumstances.

Look at how the work is designed, starting with how much difficult material each person handles and whether exposure is spread fairly. Does distressing content arrive without warning, for example graphic details in an email subject line or a forwarded file with no summary? Are caseloads and deadlines realistic? Do staff know what is expected, and do they have enough say in how they work? Is there time to recover after a critical incident, a death review or a hostile public meeting? Do people have a place to talk about the work that is not a performance conversation?

Practical changes are often small. Use approved channels for sensitive material, with a concise summary and a content note where appropriate. Preserve complete records and timely review; do not put identifying details in an email subject line. Consider rotation among qualified staff, taking workload, accommodations and required coverage into account. Arrange recovery pauses and breaks within service and staffing requirements, and clarify priorities. Consult responsible managers, Human Resources or labor relations before changing duties or schedules. Make it normal for leaders to talk about the weight of the work. When bigger mismatches exist, such as chronic understaffing, name them and raise them through management and, where relevant, labor-management channels. Well-being efforts that ignore workload tend to lose credibility quickly.
lessons.keyPoint: Chronic demands without adequate resources can contribute to burnout. Review exposure, workload, support and recovery time without assuming a single cause for a person’s distress.
lessons.example: Practice case: Omar supervises a DSD team that reviews provider licensing violations. Every morning, one inbox receives incident reports with full graphic detail in the email text, and whoever checks it first reads them all. The same two staff members, Priya and Joel, usually arrive earliest. The division has just launched a wellness challenge that awards points for steps walked. Priya mentions that she has started dreading mornings. Omar can propose changes with the responsible program and records staff. Qualified coverage, complete incident records and required reporting times must be maintained.
lessons.question: What should Omar do next?
choices: Work with the team to change how reports arrive, adding a summary and content note, rotating who triages the inbox, and scheduling a brief pause after the worst cases.
Encourage Priya to join the wellness challenge and take a walk before opening the inbox.
Ask Priya whether she needs to see a counselor before deciding what to do.
feedback: This is the strongest organizational response. It addresses uneven exposure while maintaining required review and coverage. Check whether the changes help rather than assuming they establish the cause of Priya’s distress or guarantee a fair workload.
Walking may help, but it leaves an unfair and unpredictable exposure in place for the same two people.
Offer EAP as an option without requiring counseling or health disclosure before reviewing work conditions. Organizational changes and personal support can proceed together.
lessons.reflection: Where in your work do demands most outpace resources? Which part of that gap could your team influence, and which part needs leaders?
lessons.action: Identify one way difficult material reaches your team, such as an inbox, a report queue or a meeting agenda. Propose an authorized change, such as a summary first or a planned rotation, with safeguards for complete records and timely service. Set a review after two weeks and respond sooner if problems arise.

check.question: In the NIOSH framing, what drives burnout?
check.correct: A chronic mismatch between job demands and the resources people have to meet them.
wrong: A lack of personal resilience among individual workers.
Any exposure to difficult material, regardless of workload or support.
check.feedback: NIOSH emphasizes demands and resources such as time, staffing, information and support. Individual habits help, but lasting prevention requires changing the conditions of work.

lessons.title: Supervision that sustains people
objectives: Describe supervision practices intended to support people who encounter indirect trauma through their work.
Draft check-in questions that focus on the work rather than on a person's health.
Distinguish supportive work-focused discussion from authorized medical inquiries or accommodation documentation.
Identify when to bring in Human Resources or the Employee Assistance Program.
lessons.teaching:
The National Child Traumatic Stress Network notes that individual and supervisory awareness of indirect trauma exposure is a basic part of protecting workers' health. Supervisors shape how heavy the work feels. SAMHSA's guidance for supervisors of crisis counselors lists practical steps: plan regular meetings where staff can share experiences and concerns, keep people informed about peer support and debriefing options, encourage breaks and connection with others, build buddy systems and team connection, and follow up after intense periods.

In DHS and DSD settings, that can look like regular one-to-ones with a standing question about workload and difficult cases, authorized case discussion that protects client information and does not require personal trauma disclosure, rotation among qualified staff with appropriate support, and a short team check-in after a death review, a hostile hearing or a crisis call. It also looks like modeling: taking leave, ending meetings on time, and saying out loud that a case was hard.

Keep the conversation about the work. Useful questions include: How is your workload this week? Which parts of your cases are weighing on you? What would make the next few weeks more manageable? Is there anything you would like me to change about how assignments or information reach you? An ordinary supportive check-in is not a clinical assessment. Do not guess at a diagnosis or press for symptoms or trauma history. Disability-related inquiries after employment begins generally must be job-related and consistent with business necessity; accommodation processes may need limited documentation. Consult Human Resources or the ADA coordinator about those situations. Treat volunteered medical information as confidential under applicable rules, sharing only as authorized rather than promising absolute secrecy.

If an employee's performance changes, address the work respectfully and specifically, and offer resources without guessing at the cause. You can say: I have noticed deadlines slipping this month, and I want to help. Here is how to reach the Employee Assistance Program, which is free and confidential, and if anything about your situation would benefit from a change at work, Human Resources can help with that too. If an employee asks for a change in schedule or duties for a health reason, treat it as a possible accommodation request and involve Human Resources or the ADA coordinator. For immediate danger, use the applicable emergency response. For suicidal crisis or emotional distress in the United States, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline is available by phone or text. Do not wait for a routine check-in to address an urgent concern.
lessons.keyPoint: Use supportive check-ins to discuss work and available help. Avoid speculative diagnoses, protect medical information and use authorized processes for accommodation, leave or safety concerns.
lessons.example: Practice case: Hannah supervises intake staff who take calls from families seeking disability services, some of them in crisis. One staff member, Luis, has been short with callers lately and missed two call-backs. Hannah remembers that Luis handled a call last month where a caller described a family member's death. A peer supervisor, Doug, suggests Hannah ask Luis directly whether he is dealing with trauma. Hannah has arranged the missed call-backs and checked for immediate service risks. The next step is a work-focused conversation; no urgent safety issue currently requires an immediate reassignment.
lessons.question: What should Hannah do next?
choices: Ask Luis whether he is dealing with trauma from that call so she can understand what is happening.
Meet with Luis, name the specific work issues kindly, ask what would make the workload more manageable, and offer the Employee Assistance Program and Human Resources as options.
Move Luis off the phones without discussion to protect callers.
feedback: This ordinary check-in should address the observed work issues rather than test a speculative diagnosis. A request for an accommodation or an objectively supported safety concern would be handled through the appropriate process with responsible staff.
This is the strongest response. It addresses the work honestly, invites Luis to shape a solution and offers support without requiring any disclosure.

An immediate change may be necessary for a concrete safety or service risk. In this case those concerns have been addressed, so unexplained reassignment based on Hannah’s guess is not the best next step. Discuss the work and appropriate support.
lessons.reflection: When a colleague seems to be struggling, what is your first instinct? How could you respond in a way that offers support without guessing at the cause?
lessons.action: Add one standing, work-focused question to your next round of one-to-ones or team meetings, such as: Which parts of the work are weighing on you, and what would help? Save the Employee Assistance Program contact where you can share it quickly.

check.question: During an ordinary supportive check-in, outside a formal accommodation or medical-inquiry process, which question is most appropriate?
check.correct: Which parts of your workload are weighing on you, and what would make the next few weeks more manageable?
wrong: Have you been having trouble sleeping since that difficult case?
Do you think you might have secondary traumatic stress?
check.feedback: Focus this conversation on workload and practical support rather than symptoms or a guessed condition. Formal accommodation or safety processes may require limited information through authorized channels; an ordinary check-in is not a substitute for them.

lessons.title: Support, recovery and meaning
objectives: Describe what the State of Minnesota Employee Assistance Program offers and how confidentiality works.
Identify individual recovery practices that complement organizational changes.
Plan a personal and team approach to recovery after intense work periods.
Recognize when to seek professional help or urgent support.
lessons.teaching:
Organizations are responsible for the conditions of work, and individuals still benefit from knowing what support exists and how to use it. State of Minnesota employees have an Employee Assistance Program, currently provided through LifeMatters. According to the state's current information, services are free for employees and the people they live with, available at any hour, and include confidential counseling by phone, online or in person, with up to six sessions per topic each year, as well as help with everyday life issues. Contact with the program is not shared with supervisors or Human Resources without the employee's written permission, except for legally required safety reports, including significant concerns about children or vulnerable adults. The provider explains confidentiality exceptions at intake. Check the Minnesota Management and Budget benefits pages for current details, since vendors and terms can change. Outside services recommended by EAP may have costs; ask before arranging them.

Individual practices help most when they are realistic and chosen, not assigned. SAMHSA's guidance for crisis counselors highlights adequate sleep, healthy eating, regular physical activity and active relaxation, along with staying connected to friends and family, building positive relationships with coworkers, taking breaks and time away, and having a self-care buddy or regular group check-in. A short ritual that marks the end of the workday, such as a walk, closing the laptop at a set time or a few minutes of quiet, can help separate work from home, especially for people working remotely.

Meaning matters too: many staff stay in this work because it matters to them and because they see change happen. Noticing moments of compassion satisfaction, such as a family who finally got services or a policy fix that removed a barrier, is not denial of the hard parts. Teams can make space to name what went well alongside what was hard.

Know when to reach for more help. Seek professional support when distress concerns you, persists or interferes with daily life; there is no need to wait for a fixed period. The Employee Assistance Program is one place to start, and your own health care provider is another. Use emergency procedures for immediate danger. The 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline provides phone and text support for suicidal crisis or emotional distress in the United States. You can contact EAP directly without first notifying a supervisor. A separate request for leave, an accommodation or a work change may require notice and limited information through the relevant process; Human Resources can explain those steps.
lessons.keyPoint: Combine attention to working conditions with support you choose. You can contact EAP directly; confidentiality has legal exceptions, and workplace changes follow their own processes.
lessons.example: Practice case: After a long legislative session and several difficult death reviews, a DSD policy team led by Grace is exhausted. Grace wants to help. One team member, Tomas, suggests holding a mandatory group debrief where everyone shares how the reviews affected them personally. Another, Mei, would rather take a quiet day. Grace also realizes that several people do not know the Employee Assistance Program covers the people they live with. Grace can adjust priorities within approved staffing and service requirements. The team discussion will not require personal disclosure or replace support someone chooses privately.
lessons.question: What should Grace do next?
choices: Hold the mandatory debrief so that everyone processes the experience together.
Skip any team response and trust people to find their own support.
Offer an optional team conversation about the work, protect a lighter week for recovery, and share Employee Assistance Program information with everyone.
feedback: Requiring people to share personal reactions can feel intrusive and may be harmful for some. Support should be offered, not compelled.
Leaving everything to individuals ignores what the team and leader can change after an intense period.
This is the strongest response. It gives choice, changes the workload to allow recovery and makes sure everyone knows what confidential support exists.
lessons.reflection: What helps you recover after an intense stretch of work? What gets in the way of doing it, and is any of that within your control or your team's?
lessons.action: Save the Employee Assistance Program contact in your phone, and choose one small end-of-day practice to try for two weeks. If you lead a team, plan one recovery step for after your next intense period, such as protected time or a lighter week.

check.question: According to the MMB EAP FAQ, how is contact with LifeMatters handled before any separate workplace-change request?
check.correct: No one at work, including supervisors and Human Resources, without the employee's written permission, except where the law requires a safety report.
wrong: The employee's supervisor, so that workload can be adjusted.
Human Resources, which keeps a record in the personnel file.
check.feedback: The FAQ says contact is not shared outside LifeMatters without written permission, subject to legal safety-reporting exceptions explained at intake. Workplace-change or leave requests have separate notice and documentation processes; contacting EAP does not automatically start those processes.

cards.back: Distress associated with learning about another person’s trauma. NCTSN identifies it as an occupational concern for people who work with traumatized children; the concept is relevant to other human-services work too.
An occupational challenge from continuous exposure to other people's trauma that can produce a range of negative psychological and social reactions over time.
A broad term that SAMHSA describes as a combination of burnout and secondary traumatic stress.
In WHO's definition, an occupational phenomenon from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed, with exhaustion, cynicism and reduced effectiveness. Not a medical diagnosis.
The sense of fulfillment that comes from helping others, which can exist alongside strain.

aid.heading: Team and leader changes
items: Use approved channels and a summary or content note for distressing material, preserving complete records and required review.
Consider rotation among qualified staff with appropriate coverage, workload and accommodation arrangements.
Build recovery time after critical reviews, crisis calls and hostile meetings.
Name chronic understaffing or workload gaps and raise them through management.

aid.heading: Supervisor check-ins
items: Ask about workload and which cases are weighing on people, not about symptoms.
Do not diagnose colleagues or press for personal disclosure in supportive check-ins; protect medical information and consult responsible staff about formal inquiries.
Offer the Employee Assistance Program to everyone as a routine resource.
Treat requests for schedule or duty changes for health reasons as possible accommodation requests and involve Human Resources.

aid.heading: Personal support
items: Save the Employee Assistance Program contact; it is free and confidential for you and the people you live with.
Choose a small end-of-day routine that separates work from home.
Notice moments of meaning alongside the hard parts.

Seek professional support when distress concerns you or affects daily life. Use emergency procedures for immediate danger; 988 offers phone or text support for suicidal crisis or emotional distress in the United States.
